question.value: To explore episodic accretion mechanisms, the origin of gas-phase SiO in molecular jets, and the chronologies of episodic ejection events in protostars in the Orion Molecular Cloud.

evidence.quote: To explore episodic accretion mechanisms and the chronologies of episodic events, we investigated 42 fields containing protostars with ALMA observations of CO, SiO, and 1.3 mm continuum emission.

Second, we seek to understand the origin of gas phase SiO in the jet, following the increasing evidence of SiO in the jet. Third, we probe accretion mechanisms based on the distribution of ejected material, especially the episodic knots.
we investigated 42 fields containing protostars with ALMA observations of CO, SiO, and 1.3 mm continuum emission.

analysis_steps.goal: Identify molecular jet knots, measure jet velocity (V_j, V_j,cor), and compute episodic ejection timescales (T_knot) and Keplerian perturbation radii

method.value: Search CO and SiO data cubes and PV diagrams along the flow axis to identify discrete knots; take mean velocity of brightest peak knot emission as V_j, deproject via V_j,cor = V_j / sin(i), compute mean timescale between consecutive knots as T_knot = (delta_R / V_j) tan(i), and convert T_knot to Keplerian orbital radius via Kepler's third law.

findings_qualitative.value: Out of 42 outflows detected in CO emission, SiO emission was detected in 21 fields, with 19 sources driving confirmed molecular jets (16 in this sample/study context plus previously published ALMASOP jets) and 6 sources exhibiting monopolar or nearly-monopolar SiO jets.

evidence.quote: We detected SiO emission in 21 fields, where 19 sources are driving confirmed molecular jets with high abundances of SiO.

evidence.loc: 3.5. Molecular jet detection and episodes of accretion
evidence.quote: Six of the sources exhibit monopolar or nearly-monopolar SiO jets (G203.2111.20W2, G191.90-11.20S, G205.46-14.56M1, G205.4614.56S1, G209.55-19.68S2, G211.47-19.27S B ).

findings_qualitative.value: SiO emission within knots is optically thicker than CO (tau_SiO > tau_CO), meaning CO traces deeper interior layers of the knots as well as low-density outflow shells.

evidence.quote: We estimated the optical depth for SiO ( τ SiO ) and CO ( τ CO ) emission from the peak emission within the knots, assuming a temperature T ex ∼ 150 K, and find that the SiO emission is optically thicker than that of CO ( τ SiO > τ CO ) within the knots.

findings_qualitative.value: Redshifted monopolar SiO jets can be explained by a layered internal bow-shock structure where a dense, cool compressed layer shields the middle SiO+CO layer in the blueshifted lobe from the observer.

evidence.quote: For the blue-shifted lobe, the scenario is opposite, where an observer can see only a forward CO emission front (layer i ). Emission from layers- iii and iv might be shielded by the compressed and coolest layer- ii .

claims.hypothesis: Gas-phase SiO in protostellar jets originates from dust-poor wind launched within the dust-sublimation zone rather than solely from in-situ grain sputtering.
claims.experiment: Measured SiO-to-CO abundance ratios (X_SiO/X_CO) in the innermost jet knots (B1 and R1) and compared them as a function of jet mass-loss rate against laminar 1D disk wind shock models from Tabone et al. (2020) and dust sputtering timescales.
claims.result: Observed X_SiO/X_CO ranges from ~5 x 10^-4 to 10^-2, matching dust-poor disk wind tracks, and nearest knots have dynamical timescales < 100 years.
claims.finding: Most of the SiO in the jets likely originates within the dust sublimation zone near the base of the source, although grain sputtering cannot be completely excluded at high pre-shock densities.

evidence.quote: From our observations, we see that SiO jets tend tohave X SiO /X CO in the range ∼ 5 × 10 − 4 to 10 − 2 .
We see that all the SiO jets are possibly dust-poor and hence SiO could have originated from within the dust sublimation zone of its associated protostars.

To summarize, we suggest that most of the SiO is originating within the dust sublimation zone near the base of the source. We can not, however, exclude the grainsputtering mechanism from the present state observations.

claims.hypothesis: Jet velocities, mass-loss rates, and ejection periods depend on the surrounding envelope mass and bolometric luminosity of the protostar.
claims.experiment: Performed linear regression and correlation analysis of inclination-corrected jet velocities (V_j,cor), jet mass-loss rates (Mdot_j), mean knot periods (T_knot), and outflow forces (F_CO) against ACA 1.3 mm envelope masses (M_Env) and bolometric luminosities (L_bol).
claims.result: V_j,cor and Mdot_j correlate positively with M_Env (slopes 0.21 +/- 0.14 and 0.47 +/- 0.27), T_knot is mildly anti-correlated with M_Env (slope -0.14 +/- 0.19), and F_CO correlates with both L_bol (slope 1.03 +/- 0.09) and M_env (slope 2.02 +/- 0.89).
claims.finding: Higher envelope mass around protostars increases the ejection-accretion activity (higher velocity and mass-loss rate) and triggers more frequent ejection episodes.

evidence.quote: Next, velocities and mass-loss rates are positively correlated with the surrounding envelope mass, suggesting that the presence of high mass around protostars increases the ejection-accretion activity.
Also, mean ejection periods are anti-correlated with the envelope mass, where high-accretion rates may trigger more frequent ejection events.
Outflow forces for different types of protostars and candidate FHSCs are correlated with the bolometric luminosity and envelope masses.

claims.hypothesis: Episodic accretion bursts occur frequently enough to maintain the gas-ice balance of complex organic molecules (COMs) around snowlines before they can freeze out.
claims.experiment: Compared the derived mean ejection periods (T_knot) of the jets with the theoretical freeze-out timescale of CH3OH at T ~ 100 K and n_H2 ~ 10^7 cm^-3, and compared observed CH3OH emission radii from Hsu et al. (2022) with expected 100 K sublimation radii.
claims.result: Observed ejection periods are 20 - 175 years (17 - 530 years across outburst timescales), which is much shorter than the CH3OH freeze-out timescale of ~780 years (710 - 930 years), and observed R_CH3OH values are larger than expected from current luminosities.
claims.finding: Repetitive episodic outbursts maintain outer disk temperatures and largely govern the ice-gas balance inside and around the snowline, facilitating gas-phase COM formation.

evidence.quote: The observed periods of outburst/ejection are much shorter than the freeze-out time scale of the simplest COMs like CH 3 OH, suggesting that episodic events largely maintain the ice-gas balance inside and around the snowline.

evidence.loc: 4.4.4. Episodic ejection: Implication to Complex Organic Molecule and Planet formation
evidence.quote: Based on ejection periods, the outburst time scales of 17 − 530 years for the present ALMASOP objects are less than the freeze-out time scale.

evidence.loc: 4.4.4. Episodic ejection: Implication to Complex Organic Molecule and Planet formation
evidence.quote: The large discrepancy between the methanol emission size, R CH 3 OH and the R(100) estimated from the current luminosity suggests that all sources had prior accretion bursts, and the freeze-out timescale should be longer than the time interval between episodes.

why_this_data.value: ALMASOP provides a statistically significant, unbiased sample of young, cold protostars in the Orion molecular cloud at a similar distance (~400 pc) and environment, observed at high resolution and sensitivity in 1.3 mm continuum, CO, C18O, and SiO.

evidence.quote: In this paper, we describe ALMA observations of a statically significant sample of protostars in the Orion molecular cloud. Their location in common puts them at a similar distance ( ∼ 400 pc) and in a similar environment, minimizing the effects of environmental differences on the observed parameters.
Here, we combined data from three configurations (TM1, TM2, and ACA) to improve the sensitivity of the line cubes.

why_this_method.value: ACA low-resolution continuum probes large-scale envelope mass, C18O traces systemic velocity of the inner envelope/disk, parabolic fitting to CO shells constrains inclination angle, and high-critical-density SiO (5-4) isolates dense jet knots from the CO outflow shell.

evidence.quote: In brief, we generated 1.3 mm continuum images using low-resolution ACA observations of typical beam size 7 ′′ . 6 × 4 ′′ . 1 to probe large-scale envelope emission.

evidence.loc: 3.5. Molecular jet detection and episodes of accretion
evidence.quote: Given its higher critical density and an expected increase in SiO from dust grains shattered in shocks, the SiO emission is more suitable for detecting the high-density material and shocks in the jets, where as the CO traces both high-density jet as well as low-density outflow structures.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Using ACA-only maps (FOV ~ 60'') instead of combined TM1+TM2+ACA maps (FOV ~ 40'') for F_CO measurements was rejected due to poorer sensitivity of ACA-only maps.

evidence.quote: In addition, we could not recover the whole outflow emission from the ACA maps due to their relatively poor sensitivity compared with the combined high-resolution maps. Therefore, we present only the F CO measurements derived from the high-sensitivity combined maps.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Gaussian fitting to C18O spectra to determine V_sys was rejected because the emission spans only 2-3 velocity channels.

evidence.quote: In most cases, C 18 O spread only over 2-3 channels (one channel corresponding to velocity resolution ∼ 2.0 km s − 1 ), making it challenging to get a reasonable Gaussian fit.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Binary orbital dynamics driving the accretion/ejection episodes was rejected for the wide binary systems because their separations (> 100 au) do not match the derived Keplerian perturbation radii (2 - 25 au).

evidence.quote: the Keplerian perturbation radius. Hence, it is unlikely these respective accretion/ejection events are driven by binary orbital dynamics.

limitations_admitted.value: 1.3 mm dust continuum emission may be optically thick in the central core region of extremely young protostars, so derived envelope masses represent lower limits.

evidence.quote: For an extremely young protostar, the 1.3 mm emission could be optically thick, especially in the central core region. Hence, this emission may represent a lower limit to the total dust column density from the inner envelope around the protostars.

limitations_admitted.value: The 2 km s^-1 velocity resolution is insufficient to probe the kinematics and geometry of resolved disks or to obtain Gaussian fits to C18O lines.

evidence.quote: In most cases, C 18 O spread only over 2-3 channels (one channel corresponding to velocity resolution ∼ 2.0 km s − 1 ), making it challenging to get a reasonable Gaussian fit.
In a few cases, we may have resolved the larger disks but the velocity resolution of our observations is not sufficient to probe their kinematics and geometry.

limitations_admitted.value: The parabolic outflow shell model is only suitable for objects with well-defined outflow shells that are distinguishable from ambient material or multiple outflows.

evidence.quote: Here, we note that this model is suitable only for those objects that have well-defined outflow shells, i.e., outflow walls that are well distinguished from the ambient material or outflows of multiple sources.

limitations_admitted.value: The TM1/TM2 primary beam (~40'') does not cover the full spatial extent of some outflows, and interferometric observations suffer from missing flux, optical depth, and temperature uncertainties.

evidence.quote: Here we note that we do not cover the full outflow extents within the TM1/TM2 primary beam ( ∼ 40 ′′ ).

Errors of F CO estimation depend on the amount of missing flux in interferometric observations, the lack of coverage of the full length of the outflow lobe, calibration, the optical depth of CO, the temperature variation of the outflow, and errors in the inclination angle measurements.

limitations_admitted.value: Jet widths are not spatially resolved even at ~0.38'' x 0.35'' resolution, requiring the transverse beam size to be adopted as the jet width.

evidence.loc: 3.6. Jet Mass-Loss Rate and Kinetic Luminosity
evidence.quote: Since the jet widths are not spatially resolved even at the high spatial resolution achieved, the beam size b m is taken to be the jet width.

limitations_admitted.value: SiO (5-4) and CO (2-1) can be optically thick in dense knots, making SiO-to-CO abundance ratios and jet mass-loss rates lower limits.

evidence.loc: 3.6. Jet Mass-Loss Rate and Kinetic Luminosity
evidence.quote: Therefore, we consider our measured values to be lower limits to the mass loss rates.

We note that SiO (5-4) could be optically thicker towards the dense shock than CO (2-1) in the same region. Therefore the SiO emission is likely the lower limit and the X SiO /X CO is the lower limit in this case.

referee_caveats_inferred: The linear correlations reported for log(V_j,cor), log(Mdot_j), and log(T_knot) versus log(M_Env) have large uncertainties on their slopes (0.21 +/- 0.14, 0.47 +/- 0.27, and -0.14 +/- 0.19), making them statistically weak (< 2 sigma).

Inclination angles derived from fitting parabolas to CO shells carry large uncertainties, especially for nearly edge-on sources (i <= 10 deg), which propagate nonlinearly into V_j,cor (= V_j / sin i) and T_knot (= delta_R tan i / V_j).

Assuming a single fixed dust temperature (15 K), fixed stellar mass (0.1 M_sun), and fixed stellar radius (2 R_sun) across all Class 0 and Class I protostars may introduce systematic biases in M_Env and Mdot_acc.
